# Backend Platform Team

The deep backend bench: architecture, GraphQL, event sourcing, durable workflows, test-first discipline, and someone watching the latency.

## How the team works

The flagship backend roster. The architect owns the boundaries and the contracts. The event sourcing architect decides where state should be rebuilt from history rather than mutated, and the workflow engineer owns anything long-running enough that a process restart must not lose it. GraphQL sits over the top when clients need it. The TDD orchestrator holds the loop so behaviour is specified before it is built, and the performance engineer is the one member allowed to say the design is fast enough or is not, on evidence.

## The roster

- **Backend Architect** (leads): Designs backend services and APIs with clear boundaries, explicit contracts, and resilience built in before the first endpoint ships.
- **GraphQL Architect**: Designs federated GraphQL schemas, resolver layers, and query-cost controls that stay fast as the graph grows.
- **Event Sourcing Architect**: Designs event stores, projections, and CQRS read models so that state is rebuilt from an append-only history rather than mutated in place.
- **Workflow Orchestration Engineer**: Builds durable workflows with deterministic replay, saga compensation, and activity retry policies that survive process restarts.
- **TDD Orchestrator**: Keeps a change honest by holding the red-green-refactor loop, so the test that proves the behaviour is written before the behaviour.
- **Performance Engineer**: Finds where the time actually goes with profiles and load tests, then fixes the one bottleneck that moves the number.

## Handoffs

- Backend Architect to Event Sourcing Architect, when a domain needs an auditable history rather than a current-state row.
- Backend Architect to Workflow Orchestration Engineer, when a process spans minutes or days and must survive a restart.
- GraphQL Architect to Backend Architect, when the schema is being shaped by the wrong service boundaries.
- Event Sourcing Architect to TDD Orchestrator, when the projection behaviour needs to be pinned before it is written.
- Workflow Orchestration Engineer to Performance Engineer, when a workflow is slower than the business process it models.
- TDD Orchestrator to Backend Architect, when a test cannot be written cleanly because the design fights it.
- Performance Engineer to GraphQL Architect, when the slow path is a query shape rather than the code behind it.

wshobson-c4-documentation.workflowNarrative:
# C4 Documentation Line

Four documenters that work the C4 levels in order, from reading the source up to the system context diagram.

## How the team works

The routing order is the method. This team works bottom up: the code documenter reads the source and records what is actually there, the component documenter groups those findings into responsibilities, the container documenter maps components onto deployable units, and the context documenter draws the outermost view of the system and its neighbours. Each level takes the level below as input, so no one invents a box that nothing underneath supports. Run it in reverse and you get the architecture somebody wishes existed.

## The roster

- **C4 Code Documenter**: Documents the lowest C4 level by reading source directly: classes, modules, and the relationships the code actually has.
- **C4 Component Documenter**: Rolls code-level findings up into components, naming each responsibility and the interfaces between them.
- **C4 Container Documenter**: Maps components onto deployable containers: the applications, data stores, and the protocols connecting them.
- **C4 Context Documenter** (leads): Draws the outermost C4 view: the system, the people who use it, and every external system it depends on.

## Handoffs

- C4 Code Documenter to C4 Component Documenter, when the code-level pass is complete.
- C4 Component Documenter to C4 Container Documenter, when the components and their interfaces are documented.
- C4 Container Documenter to C4 Context Documenter, when the containers and their connections are documented.
- C4 Context Documenter to C4 Code Documenter, when the context view reveals a dependency nothing in the code explains.

wshobson-cloud-infrastructure.workflowNarrative:
# Cloud Infrastructure Team

Designs and runs the estate itself: cloud architecture, hybrid placement, clusters, networking, service mesh, and the code that describes it.

## How the team works

Where the delivery crew owns the pipeline, this team owns the ground it deploys onto. The cloud architect sets the shape and the cost model. The hybrid architect handles anything that will not or cannot live in one provider. Kubernetes and the service mesh own workload scheduling and service-to-service traffic, the network engineer owns everything below that, and the Terraform specialist makes sure all of it is described in code rather than in somebody memory.

## The roster

- **Cloud Architect** (leads): Designs cloud infrastructure across major providers with infrastructure as code and a cost model that survives contact with the bill.
- **Hybrid Cloud Architect**: Designs estates that span public cloud and private data centres, with workload placement, connectivity, and migration paths mapped out.
- **Kubernetes Architect**: Designs Kubernetes platforms with GitOps delivery, sane multi-tenancy, and cluster policy that developers can work inside.
- **Terraform Specialist**: Writes reusable infrastructure modules and manages state, drift, and imports so plans stay readable and applies stay boring.
- **Network Engineer**: Diagnoses and designs cloud networking: routing, DNS, load balancers, TLS termination, and the latency nobody can account for.
- **Service Mesh Engineer**: Runs service-to-service traffic through a mesh: routing rules, mutual TLS, retries, and the observability that comes with them.

## Handoffs

- Cloud Architect to Terraform Specialist, when the target architecture is agreed.
- Cloud Architect to Hybrid Cloud Architect, when a workload cannot leave a private data centre.
- Hybrid Cloud Architect to Network Engineer, when the design depends on links between sites.
- Kubernetes Architect to Service Mesh Engineer, when services need identity, retries, and traffic control between them.
- Terraform Specialist to Kubernetes Architect, when the cluster itself needs to be provisioned.
- Network Engineer to Cloud Architect, when the network design constrains the architecture.
- Service Mesh Engineer to Cloud Architect, when the mesh cost is material at the current scale.

wshobson-comprehensive-review.workflowNarrative:
# Multi-Angle Review Panel

Three readers on one change: one for the code, one for the architecture it lands in, and one for what an attacker would do with it.

## How the team works

One change, three angles, deliberately kept apart. The code reviewer reads the diff for correctness and maintenance cost. The architecture reviewer asks whether the change fits the system it lands in or quietly bends it. The security auditor asks what an attacker reaches through it. Keeping the passes separate is the point: a single reader trades one concern off against another without noticing, and the code reviewer is the one who merges the three into a single verdict.

## The roster

- **Code Reviewer** (leads): Reviews a change for correctness, security, and the maintenance cost it creates, and says which findings actually block a merge.
- **Architecture Reviewer**: Reviews a change against the architecture it lands in: boundaries, coupling, and whether the pattern earns its complexity.
- **Security Auditor**: Audits a system for exploitable weaknesses and compliance gaps, and ranks findings by what an attacker would actually reach first.

## Handoffs

- Code Reviewer to Architecture Reviewer, when a change is locally correct but sits oddly in the system.
- Code Reviewer to Security Auditor, when a change touches authentication, personal data, money, or untrusted input.
- Architecture Reviewer to Code Reviewer, when the architectural pass is complete.
- Security Auditor to Code Reviewer, when the security pass is complete.

wshobson-database-optimization.workflowNarrative:
# Database Optimisation Team

Picks the right store, models the schema, tunes the queries, and checks what the whole thing costs to run.

## How the team works

The order matters here, because most database pain is a modelling decision showing up as a slow query six months later. The architect chooses the store and the schema against the real access patterns. The optimiser and the SQL specialist work the existing system: read the plan, fix the index or the statement, prove the improvement. The cloud architect is in the room because storage and IO are usually the line on the bill nobody predicted.

## The roster

- **Database Architect** (leads): Chooses the data store and designs the schema before the first migration, weighing access patterns against operational cost.
- **Database Optimizer**: Finds the slow query, reads the plan, fixes the index or the query, and proves the improvement with measurements.
- **SQL Specialist**: Writes SQL that the planner likes: window functions, CTE discipline, index-aware predicates, and honest execution plans.
- **Cloud Architect**: Designs cloud infrastructure across major providers with infrastructure as code and a cost model that survives contact with the bill.

## Handoffs

- Database Architect to SQL Specialist, when the schema is settled and the access patterns need real queries.
- Database Optimizer to Database Architect, when a query cannot be made fast without changing the model.
- SQL Specialist to Database Optimizer, when a statement is correct but the plan is bad.
- Cloud Architect to Database Architect, when the storage or IO cost is out of proportion to the workload.
- Database Architect to Cloud Architect, when the design implies a managed service choice.

wshobson-delivery-pipeline.workflowNarrative:
# Delivery Pipeline Crew

Builds the path from commit to production: pipeline configuration, infrastructure code, cluster delivery, and someone who debugs it at 3am.

## How the team works

This team owns the pipeline rather than the estate. The deployment engineer designs the path a commit takes to production, including the verification step and the rehearsed rollback. The cloud architect says what the target environment should look like, the Terraform specialist expresses it as reviewable code, and the Kubernetes architect owns delivery into the cluster. The troubleshooter is the member who has to live with all of it at three in the morning, and has a standing veto on anything that cannot be diagnosed under pressure.

## The roster

- **Deployment Engineer** (leads): Builds the pipeline from commit to production: progressive rollout, automated verification, and a rollback that has been rehearsed.
- **Cloud Architect**: Designs cloud infrastructure across major providers with infrastructure as code and a cost model that survives contact with the bill.
- **Terraform Specialist**: Writes reusable infrastructure modules and manages state, drift, and imports so plans stay readable and applies stay boring.
- **Kubernetes Architect**: Designs Kubernetes platforms with GitOps delivery, sane multi-tenancy, and cluster policy that developers can work inside.
- **DevOps Troubleshooter**: Works a live production problem from symptom to cause using logs, metrics, and traces, and stabilises before it explains.

## Handoffs

- Deployment Engineer to Terraform Specialist, when the pipeline needs infrastructure that does not exist yet.
- Deployment Engineer to Kubernetes Architect, when the release target is a cluster.
- Cloud Architect to Deployment Engineer, when the target environment design is settled.
- Terraform Specialist to Cloud Architect, when the modules reveal an ambiguity in the intended architecture.
- Kubernetes Architect to DevOps Troubleshooter, when a rollout behaves differently in the cluster than in staging.
- DevOps Troubleshooter to Deployment Engineer, when an incident traces back to the release path.

wshobson-documentation-generation.workflowNarrative:
# Documentation Team

Turns a codebase into documentation people actually use: the long-form architecture piece, the API spec, the reference, and the tutorial.

## How the team works

Four different documents, four different readers, and they are not interchangeable. The documentation architect writes the long-form piece that explains why the system is shaped the way it is. The API documenter produces the specification a caller works from. The reference builder produces the exhaustive listing someone scans for a single fact. The tutorial author produces the ordered path a newcomer follows. Writing one of these when the reader needed another is the most common documentation failure, and the architect is the member who decides which is needed.

## The roster

- **Documentation Architect** (leads): Reads a codebase and produces the long-form document it never had: architecture, decisions, and the reasoning behind both.
- **API Documenter**: Writes API documentation people can work from: an accurate specification, real examples, and error cases that are not hidden.
- **Reference Builder**: Builds exhaustive reference material: every parameter, every return, every constraint, arranged so a reader can scan for one fact.
- **Tutorial Author**: Turns a working system into a lesson: an ordered path, one new idea per step, and a reader who can run every example.

## Handoffs

- Documentation Architect to API Documenter, when the system exposes an interface other people call.
- Documentation Architect to Tutorial Author, when a newcomer needs a path rather than an explanation.
- API Documenter to Reference Builder, when the specification is complete but the parameter detail is thin.
- Reference Builder to Documentation Architect, when the reference exposes behaviour that no document explains.
- Tutorial Author to API Documenter, when an example in the lesson does not match the documented interface.

wshobson-incident-response.workflowNarrative:
# Incident Response Team

Runs a live production incident: someone commanding it, someone reading the logs, someone finding the cause, and someone stabilising the system.

## How the team works

Roles are separated on purpose, because the most common way an incident goes badly is one person trying to command, investigate and fix at once. The incident responder declares severity, keeps the timeline, and owns communication. The troubleshooter works the live system to restore service. The error detective reads logs and traces to establish scope and start time. The debugger takes the eventual root cause hunt, and the observability engineer makes sure the next one is easier to see. Restore first, explain after.

## The roster

- **Incident Responder** (leads): Runs an incident: declares severity, restores service first, keeps the comms trail, and writes the blameless postmortem after.
- **DevOps Troubleshooter**: Works a live production problem from symptom to cause using logs, metrics, and traces, and stabilises before it explains.
- **Error Detective**: Reads error traces and logs to reconstruct what happened: the signature, the blast radius, the timeline, and the reproduction.
- **Root Cause Debugger**: Traces a production bug to the exact line and commit that caused it, testing hypotheses instead of guessing at fixes.
- **Observability Engineer**: Builds metrics, logging, and tracing that answer real questions, with SLOs and alerts tied to what users actually feel.

## Handoffs

- Incident Responder to DevOps Troubleshooter, when service is degraded and needs stabilising now.
- Incident Responder to Error Detective, when the blast radius and the start time are unknown.
- DevOps Troubleshooter to Incident Responder, when service is stable again.
- Error Detective to Root Cause Debugger, when the failure signature is isolated but the cause is not.
- Root Cause Debugger to Incident Responder, when the root cause is established.
- Observability Engineer to Incident Responder, when the incident was slow to detect.

wshobson-interface-design.workflowNarrative:
# Interface Design Team

Designs the interface and the system behind it: component anatomy, the token layer, and an accessibility pass that happens before handoff.

## How the team works

The product designer owns the reasoning: what the user is trying to do and why the flow is shaped this way. The UI designer turns that into concrete component work, including the states everyone forgets. The design system architect makes sure the result is expressed in tokens and components rather than in one-off values, so the next screen is cheaper. The accessibility specialist reviews before handoff rather than after, because retrofitting is where accessibility work usually dies.

## The roster

- **Product Designer** (leads): Moves from user research to wireframes to a documented design system, keeping the reasoning attached to every screen.
- **UI Designer**: Turns product intent into concrete interface work: component anatomy, layout systems, spacing scales, and states nobody remembered.
- **Design System Architect**: Builds the token layer, component contracts, and theming infrastructure that let a design system survive more than one product.
- **Accessibility Specialist**: Audits and fixes interfaces against WCAG, testing with real assistive technology rather than an automated score alone.

## Handoffs

- Product Designer to UI Designer, when the flow and the reasoning are settled.
- UI Designer to Design System Architect, when a screen needs a component or a value the system does not have.
- Design System Architect to Product Designer, when a request would fork the system for one screen.
- Accessibility Specialist to UI Designer, when a design fails contrast, target size, or focus order.

wshobson-jvm-and-dotnet.workflowNarrative:
# JVM and .NET Bench

Three managed-runtime specialists for enterprise codebases: Java, Scala, and C#, with the runtime tuning that goes with them.

## How the team works

A peer team with no lead, because the right member is decided by the file extension rather than by seniority. What they share is a managed runtime, a garbage collector with opinions, and a large body of existing enterprise code that cannot simply be rewritten. They consult each other on the problems that cross runtimes: concurrency models, allocation behaviour under load, and how far a codebase can be modernised without a rewrite nobody has budget for.

## The roster

- **Java Specialist**: Writes modern Java with virtual threads, records, and pattern matching, and tunes the JVM for the workload it actually runs.
- **Scala Specialist**: Writes functional Scala for distributed and big-data workloads, with effect systems, typed streams, and pragmatic purity.
- **C# Specialist**: Writes modern C# with records, pattern matching, and async pipelines, and profiles .NET allocations before reaching for tricks.

## Handoffs

- Java Specialist to Scala Specialist, when the work moves into functional or streaming code on the same runtime.
- Scala Specialist to Java Specialist, when the interop surface with existing Java code is the hard part.
- C# Specialist to Java Specialist, when a pattern needs porting between the two ecosystems.

wshobson-llm-application.workflowNarrative:
# LLM Application Team

Builds an LLM feature that survives production: retrieval that returns the right chunk, prompts that are measured, and context that is managed.

## How the team works

Most LLM features fail for one of three reasons: the retrieval returned the wrong chunk, the prompt was changed on a hunch, or the context window filled with noise. This team assigns each of those to a member. The AI engineer owns the system and its failure behaviour. The vector database engineer owns embedding, chunking and recall. The prompt engineer owns everything that goes in the instruction, evaluated against a fixed set rather than by feel. The context engineer decides what is kept, summarised and dropped between turns.

## The roster

- **AI Applications Engineer** (leads): Builds LLM applications that hold up in production: retrieval that returns the right chunk, tool calls that fail safely, and cost control.
- **Vector Database Engineer**: Chooses the embedding model, the index type, and the chunking strategy, then tunes recall and latency against real queries.
- **Prompt Engineer**: Designs and tests prompts against a measurable outcome, so a change to the wording is judged by a score rather than a vibe.
- **Context Engineer**: Manages what an AI system knows at each turn: what to retrieve, what to summarise, what to keep, and what to forget.

## Handoffs

- AI Applications Engineer to Vector Database Engineer, when the model answers confidently from the wrong source material.
- AI Applications Engineer to Prompt Engineer, when the behaviour needs to change and the retrieval is already correct.
- Vector Database Engineer to Context Engineer, when recall is good but the retrieved material overflows the window.
- Prompt Engineer to AI Applications Engineer, when no prompt change moves the score.
- Context Engineer to AI Applications Engineer, when the system is spending most of its budget on context it never uses.

wshobson-llm-finetuning.workflowNarrative:
# Fine-Tuning Team

An eval-gated fine-tuning line: the strategist decides whether to train at all, the eval engineer holds the gate, the training engineer runs it.

## How the team works

The gate is the whole design. The architect refuses to plan a training run without a baseline and a written evaluation, because most fine-tuning projects that fail were never measurable in the first place. The eval engineer builds the golden sets and the graders, calibrates the judges, and is the only member who can call a checkpoint better. The training engineer prepares the data, runs the job and exports artifacts, and reports the honest curve rather than the flattering one.

## The roster

- **Fine-Tuning Architect** (leads): Decides whether to fine-tune at all, and if so which method and base model, refusing to start without a baseline and an eval gate.
- **Fine-Tuning Eval Engineer**: Builds the golden sets and graders that decide whether a checkpoint is better, and calibrates the judges before trusting them.
- **Fine-Tuning Training Engineer**: Prepares datasets, writes and launches the training run, watches the loss curves, and exports artifacts that can be served.

## Handoffs

- Fine-Tuning Architect to Fine-Tuning Eval Engineer, when a method and a base model have been chosen.
- Fine-Tuning Eval Engineer to Fine-Tuning Training Engineer, when the baseline and the gate are established.
- Fine-Tuning Training Engineer to Fine-Tuning Eval Engineer, when a checkpoint is ready.
- Fine-Tuning Eval Engineer to Fine-Tuning Architect, when no checkpoint clears the gate.

wshobson-machine-learning-ops.workflowNarrative:
# Machine Learning Ops Team

Takes a model from analysis to a served, monitored, reproducible system: the science, the serving, and the pipeline around both.

## How the team works

The handoff from analysis to production is where most machine learning work dies, so this team names it explicitly. The data engineer supplies the pipeline and the contracts the data arrives under. The data scientist works the problem and reports the honest result with its limits. The machine learning engineer turns the chosen model into a served system with versioning and drift monitoring. The MLOps engineer owns reproducibility across all of it: if a result cannot be reproduced, it is not a result.

## The roster

- **Data Scientist**: Turns a business question into an analysis: the right statistical method, an honest read of the result, and its limits stated.
- **Machine Learning Engineer**: Takes a model from notebook to production service: serving, batching, versioning, and the monitoring that catches drift.
- **MLOps Engineer** (leads): Builds the pipeline around the model: reproducible training runs, experiment tracking, a model registry, and automated promotion.
- **Data Engineer**: Builds batch and streaming pipelines into a warehouse or lakehouse, with schema contracts and data quality checks in the path.

## Handoffs

- Data Engineer to Data Scientist, when the pipeline delivers the data with quality checks in the path.
- Data Scientist to Machine Learning Engineer, when a model beats the baseline by a margin worth serving.
- Machine Learning Engineer to MLOps Engineer, when a model is ready to be promoted.
- MLOps Engineer to Data Engineer, when a training run cannot be reproduced because the input data moved.

wshobson-multi-platform-product.workflowNarrative:
# Multi-Platform Product Team

Ships one product across web, iOS and Android against a shared API contract, with a designer keeping the surfaces coherent.

## How the team works

The hard part of multi-platform work is not any one client, it is keeping four surfaces honest against one contract. The backend architect owns that contract and publishes it before the clients start. The designer owns the coherence of the surfaces so they feel like one product rather than three teams. The client members each own their platform and are expected to push back early when the contract will force awkward code on their side, rather than quietly working around it.

## The roster

- **Backend Architect** (leads): Designs backend services and APIs with clear boundaries, explicit contracts, and resilience built in before the first endpoint ships.
- **Frontend Developer**: Builds React interfaces with sane state boundaries, responsive layouts, and rendering costs measured rather than guessed.
- **iOS Developer**: Builds native iOS apps in Swift and SwiftUI, with Core Data persistence, background work, and App Store release discipline.
- **Mobile Developer**: Builds cross-platform mobile apps with offline-first data, native module bridges, and release pipelines for both stores.
- **Flutter Developer**: Builds Flutter apps with a chosen state-management story, custom render work where it pays, and one codebase across platforms.
- **Product Designer**: Moves from user research to wireframes to a documented design system, keeping the reasoning attached to every screen.

## Handoffs

- Backend Architect to Frontend Developer, when the contract is published.
- Product Designer to Backend Architect, when a design implies data the contract does not carry.
- Frontend Developer to Product Designer, when a state in the flow has no design.
- iOS Developer to Backend Architect, when the client needs four round trips where it should need one.
- Mobile Developer to iOS Developer, when a platform behaviour needs native work behind the shared layer.
- Flutter Developer to Mobile Developer, when the shared codebase cannot express a platform difference cleanly.

wshobson-observability.workflowNarrative:
# Observability Team

Makes a running system legible: metrics, logs and traces that answer real questions, with alerts tied to what users feel.

## How the team works

Instrumentation is only worth its cost if it answers a question someone actually asks during an incident. The observability engineer designs for those questions and sets service objectives against what users feel rather than what is convenient to measure. The other three members are the people who consume the signal: the performance engineer for latency, the network engineer for everything between the boxes, and the database optimiser for the query layer, which is where slow systems usually turn out to be slow.

## The roster

- **Observability Engineer** (leads): Builds metrics, logging, and tracing that answer real questions, with SLOs and alerts tied to what users actually feel.
- **Performance Engineer**: Finds where the time actually goes with profiles and load tests, then fixes the one bottleneck that moves the number.
- **Network Engineer**: Diagnoses and designs cloud networking: routing, DNS, load balancers, TLS termination, and the latency nobody can account for.
- **Database Optimizer**: Finds the slow query, reads the plan, fixes the index or the query, and proves the improvement with measurements.

## Handoffs

- Observability Engineer to Performance Engineer, when the traces show latency without an obvious owner.
- Performance Engineer to Database Optimizer, when the time is going into the data layer.
- Network Engineer to Observability Engineer, when a latency source sits between services rather than inside one.
- Database Optimizer to Observability Engineer, when the query layer needs instrumentation it does not have.

wshobson-operating-kit.workflowNarrative:
# Operating Kit

A portable working method: open the session with verified state, review before shipping, deploy with proof, and close with an honest handover.

## How the team works

This team is a loop rather than a hierarchy, and it is the one to reach for when work spans many sessions or many people. The session opener reconciles the recorded state against live reality and names the next action. The pre-ship reviewer sweeps everything changed since the last deploy. The deploy verifier ships and proves it. The log checker reads production afterwards and separates new noise from old. The session closer writes the handover, including what broke and what was left unfinished, which is what the opener will read next time.

## The roster

- **Session Opener** (leads): Opens a work session by reading the state document, checking it against live reality, and naming the one thing to do next.
- **Pre-Ship Reviewer**: Sweeps everything changed since the last deploy and reports what is safe to ship, what needs a second look, and what must not go out.
- **Deploy Verifier**: Runs a deploy end to end and proves it landed: tests, build, release, live checks, and the record of what changed.
- **Production Log Checker**: Pulls recent production logs, separates the new noise from the known noise, and reports what changed since the last deploy.
- **Session Closer**: Closes a work session by recording what changed, what broke, what is still open, and what the next session should pick up.

## Handoffs

- Session Opener to Pre-Ship Reviewer, when a body of work looks ready to go out.
- Pre-Ship Reviewer to Deploy Verifier, when the review found nothing that blocks.
- Deploy Verifier to Production Log Checker, when the release has settled.
- Production Log Checker to Session Closer, when production looks the way it should.
- Session Closer to Session Opener, when the session is closing with work still open.

wshobson-parallel-delivery-squad.workflowNarrative:
# Parallel Delivery Squad

A lead who splits the work, an implementer who builds inside strict file boundaries, a reviewer, and a debugger for when it goes wrong.

## How the team works

This is the reference team shape. The lead decomposes a request into tasks with non-overlapping file ownership and assigns them. The implementer builds inside its assigned boundary and reports at the integration points it was given. The reviewer takes one dimension at a time and reports findings in a fixed shape, so two reviews never argue about format. The debugger is held in reserve: when something fails, it takes a single hypothesis and tries to falsify it rather than joining a general hunt. Everything comes back to the lead, who produces one answer rather than four reports.

## The roster

- **Team Lead** (leads): Breaks work into parallel tasks with clear file ownership, runs the team through them, and synthesises the results into one answer.
- **Team Implementer**: Builds one assigned component inside strict file boundaries and coordinates only at the integration points it was given.
- **Team Reviewer**: Reviews a change along one assigned dimension and reports findings in a fixed format, so parallel reviews merge without arguing.
- **Team Debugger**: Takes one hypothesis about a bug and tries to falsify it, reporting the evidence with file and line citations and a confidence level.

## Handoffs

- Team Lead to Team Implementer, when the work has been split into tasks with clear file ownership.
- Team Lead to Team Reviewer, when an implementation is ready and needs checking.
- Team Implementer to Team Lead, when a component is finished or blocked at an integration point.
- Team Implementer to Team Debugger, when the build fails for a reason you cannot see from inside your boundary.
- Team Reviewer to Team Lead, when a review is complete.
- Team Debugger to Team Lead, when a hypothesis has been confirmed or ruled out.

wshobson-python-development.workflowNarrative:
# Python Development Team

Modern Python across the two dominant web stacks, with a language specialist for everything below the framework.

## How the team works

A small, deliberately narrow team. The Python specialist owns the language layer: typing, async behaviour, packaging, and the profiling that decides whether an optimisation is worth doing. The framework specialists own their respective stacks and know when the framework is the wrong tool. The most useful thing this team does is refuse to answer a framework question with a language answer, or the reverse.

## The roster

- **Python Specialist** (leads): Writes modern Python with real type coverage, async where it pays, and profiling before optimisation.
- **Django Specialist**: Builds Django applications with async views, a well-modelled ORM layer, background task queues, and real deployment settings.
- **FastAPI Specialist**: Builds high-throughput async APIs with typed request models, dependency injection, and connection pooling that holds under load.

## Handoffs

- Python Specialist to Django Specialist, when the work is a batteries-included web application.
- Python Specialist to FastAPI Specialist, when the work is an async or high-throughput API.
- Django Specialist to Python Specialist, when the bottleneck is beneath the framework.
- FastAPI Specialist to Python Specialist, when async behaviour is producing results nobody can explain.

wshobson-security-research.workflowNarrative:
# Security Research Team

Defensive analysis of things without source: binaries, hostile samples, and shipped firmware, for authorised research only.

## How the team works

This team works defensively and only on systems the user is authorised to examine. The reverse engineer reads binaries without source. The malware analyst studies hostile samples to produce indicators and detection rules a defender can deploy. The firmware analyst covers embedded and hardware products, where the update channel is usually the weakest part. The threat modeller leads, because the point of the work is a ranked, actionable picture of risk rather than an interesting finding nobody acts on.

## The roster

- **Reverse Engineer**: Reads binaries without source: disassembly, decompilation, and dynamic analysis to work out what a program really does.
- **Malware Analyst**: Analyses hostile samples for defence: behaviour, indicators of compromise, and the detection rules a team can deploy today.
- **Firmware Analyst**: Pulls apart embedded firmware to find the weaknesses in IoT and hardware products, from bootloader to update channel.
- **Threat Modeller** (leads): Runs a structured threat model over a design, naming the trust boundaries, the plausible attacks, and the mitigations worth building.

## Handoffs

- Threat Modeller to Reverse Engineer, when a component has no source and the model needs to know what it does.
- Reverse Engineer to Malware Analyst, when the sample appears to be deliberately hostile.
- Malware Analyst to Threat Modeller, when the indicators are extracted.
- Firmware Analyst to Threat Modeller, when a device weakness is confirmed.

wshobson-seo-content.workflowNarrative:
# SEO Content Studio

Plans the cluster, writes the pieces, and audits what already exists, so publishing follows a plan instead of a hunch.

## How the team works

This is the creation half of search work. The planner turns a topic into a cluster with a pillar, supporting pieces, and the internal links drawn before anything is written. The writer works from the brief and is expected to push back when an optimisation would damage the piece for a human reader. The auditor scores what already exists and says which pages deserve a refresh rather than a rewrite. The content marketer makes sure every piece has somewhere to go once it is published.

## The roster

- **SEO Content Planner** (leads): Turns a topic into a cluster plan: the pillar page, the supporting articles, the internal links, and the order to publish them.
- **SEO Content Writer**: Writes from a keyword brief without writing for a robot: the search intent is served and the piece still reads like prose.
- **SEO Content Auditor**: Scores existing content on quality and experience signals, then lists the specific edits that would move it.
- **Content Marketer**: Plans and writes content against a distribution plan, so every piece has a channel, an audience, and a way to be measured.

## Handoffs

- SEO Content Planner to SEO Content Writer, when a brief is ready with its intent and its supporting pieces.
- SEO Content Writer to SEO Content Auditor, when a draft is finished.
- SEO Content Auditor to SEO Content Planner, when an audit shows a cluster is thin or duplicated.
- Content Marketer to SEO Content Planner, when a campaign needs supporting content that does not exist.

wshobson-seo-technical.workflowNarrative:
# Technical SEO Team

The mechanical half of search: keyword use, metadata within its limits, page structure and schema, and formatting that wins result features.

## How the team works

Everything here is checkable, which is why it is kept apart from the writing team. The structure architect leads because heading hierarchy, schema and internal linking are the constraints the other three work inside. The keyword strategist checks how a page uses its terms and flags over-optimisation. The meta optimiser writes titles and descriptions that fit the limits and still earn a click. The snippet hunter reshapes answers into the formats a result box will lift, and is expected to say when that would make the page worse.

## The roster

- **SEO Keyword Strategist**: Analyses how a page uses its keywords, flags over-optimisation, and suggests the semantic variants the topic is missing.
- **SEO Meta Optimizer**: Writes titles, descriptions, and URL slugs that fit the character limits and still give a reader a reason to click.
- **SEO Structure Architect** (leads): Fixes the shape of a page and a site: heading hierarchy, schema markup, and the internal links that spread authority.
- **SEO Snippet Hunter**: Reformats content into the shapes search engines lift into featured snippets: direct answers, tables, and ordered steps.

## Handoffs

- SEO Structure Architect to SEO Snippet Hunter, when a page has a question worth owning outright.
- SEO Keyword Strategist to SEO Structure Architect, when two pages are competing for the same query.
- SEO Meta Optimizer to SEO Keyword Strategist, when the title cannot carry every term someone wants in it.
- SEO Snippet Hunter to SEO Meta Optimizer, when a page now answers directly and the metadata still promises a list.

wshobson-ship-it.workflowNarrative:
# Ship It Crew

The gate before a release: automated tests, a security pass, a performance check, and a deploy that is verified rather than assumed.

## How the team works

End-to-end release orchestration. The test automator establishes that the change does what it claims. The security auditor and the performance engineer each hold a veto in their own area, exercised on evidence rather than on instinct. The deployment engineer owns the path to production and the rehearsed rollback, and the deploy verifier proves afterwards that what is running is what was intended. Nothing here is a rubber stamp: each member has to produce the check it ran.

## The roster

- **Test Automation Engineer**: Builds the test pyramid that a team can live with: fast unit coverage, meaningful integration tests, and end-to-end suites that stay green.
- **Security Auditor**: Audits a system for exploitable weaknesses and compliance gaps, and ranks findings by what an attacker would actually reach first.
- **Performance Engineer**: Finds where the time actually goes with profiles and load tests, then fixes the one bottleneck that moves the number.
- **Deployment Engineer** (leads): Builds the pipeline from commit to production: progressive rollout, automated verification, and a rollback that has been rehearsed.
- **Deploy Verifier**: Runs a deploy end to end and proves it landed: tests, build, release, live checks, and the record of what changed.

## Handoffs

- Test Automation Engineer to Security Auditor, when the change touches credentials, personal data, money, or untrusted input.
- Security Auditor to Deployment Engineer, when the security pass is complete.
- Performance Engineer to Deployment Engineer, when a change regresses latency or throughput against the baseline.
- Deployment Engineer to Deploy Verifier, when the release has gone out.
- Deploy Verifier to Deployment Engineer, when the live check disagrees with what was expected.

wshobson-systems-programming.workflowNarrative:
# Systems Programming Bench

Low-level and performance-critical work: Rust and Go for the services, and defensive shell for everything that automates around them.

## How the team works

A peer team with no lead. Rust and Go cover the same ground from opposite directions: Rust when the memory and concurrency guarantees are worth the compile-time argument, Go when a service should be boring to operate and quick to hand over. The shell specialist is here because systems work always grows a layer of automation around it, and that layer is usually the least defensive code in the repository.

## The roster

- **Rust Specialist**: Writes Rust that satisfies the borrow checker by design rather than by fighting it, with async runtimes and zero-cost abstractions.
- **Go Specialist**: Writes idiomatic Go with disciplined concurrency, explicit error handling, and services that are boring to operate.
- **Shell Automation Engineer**: Writes defensive shell for automation that runs unattended: strict modes, safe quoting, traps, and scripts that are actually testable.

## Handoffs

- Rust Specialist to Go Specialist, when the service does not need the guarantees Rust is charging for.
- Go Specialist to Rust Specialist, when the hot path needs control over allocation and lifetimes.
- Shell Automation Engineer to Go Specialist, when a script has grown into something that needs tests and types.
